title: MN Peatland Carbon Modeling
text:
1 Preface
This e-book documents the methods and workflow for the peatland carbon modeling component of the MN School Trust Legislative Directive to UMN Department of Forest Resources and UMN Department of Soil, Water and Climate.

title: MN Peatland Carbon Modeling
text:
1.1 Project Description
This project produces 10m raster maps of peatland extent and characteristics across Minnesota. Point observations from the Minnesota DNR Peat Inventory, National Soil Information System (NASIS), and Minnesota Biological Survey data, along with a stack of 172 candidate covariates were used to develop gradient-boosting models to predict (1) the probability of peat presence, (2) peat depth, and (3) the proportions of fibric, hemic, and sapric material in the upper meter of the profile. The probability model which maps ~7.85 million acres of peatlands is used as a mask for all other property layers. Peat depth is then converted to a full-profile carbon stock using a depth-to-carbon relationship fitted to Peat Inventory pedons. Models were evaluated with 50 km spatial block cross-validation as well as random cross-validation. This ebook documents the data, methods, and results of that mapping workflow.

title: 2  Point Data Curation
text:
2.0.1 Point Data Sources
Peat presence, depth, and decomposition models were trained using soil observation data from three main sources: the Minnesota Peat Inventory, the National Soil Information System (NAISIS), and the Minnesota Biological Survey (MBS).
The Minnesota Peat Inventory is a dataset collected by the Minnesota DNR during the 1970’s and 1980’s. It contains probe measurement peat depths across peatlands in Minnesota as well as laboratory analyzed data including von post decomposition class, bulk density, carbon content, ash content, and other metrics at a horizon level.
NASIS is the USDA’s Natural Resource Conservation Services data set that populates soil survey. The dataset contains soil profile descriptions of both mineral and organic soils across the country.
The Minnesota Biological Survey contributes presence and absence observations derived from native plant community classifications where peat associated community types were coded as peat present and upland (non peat) communities were coded as peat absent.
Together, these sources created a spatially distributed dataset across the state. The point datasets contained the following number of observations:

title: 2  Point Data Curation
text:
2.1 Data Curation Methods
The final point datasets used to train each model were created by combining the data sources and applying filters specific to each variable.

2.1.1 Binary Presence/Absence Dataset
FINAL_binary_mn.csv (~60,000 points) This is the point dataset used for binary peat classification models. It combines all points from the Minnesota peat inventory, NASIS and the MBS. A new field was created called peat_binary. Organic points from the Peat Inventory and NASIS, and MBS points within peatland communities get a value of 1. Mineral points from NASIS and points from the MBS outside of peatland communities are assigned a 0. peat_binary 1 (peat present) or 0 (peat absent).
A secondary version (FINAL_binary_mn_0_20_dropped.csv) excludes points from NASIS and the Peat Inventory where peat depth was measured between 1–20 cm. These are soils that may have a described organic “O” horizon but do not indicate a Histosol. (57,134)


2.1.2 Peat Depth Dataset
depb_points_mn.csv (45,878 points) A dataset of locations that have confirmed peat depth measurements (depb in cm). Unlike the binary dataset, every point within this set has a measured depth value. This dataset is used for depth prediction models. Only non peat values with a MEASURED value of 0cm were added to this set (NASIS mineral points, mn peat inventory). All MBS points were excluded. Of the 45,878 points, 10,909 have a depth greater than 0 cm. In the combined probability dataset (57,134 points, binary_peat_features_s1_combined.csv), 45,658 points have a depth value and 8,550 of those are greater than 0 cm. The 8,223 points used to train the final depth models are the points with depb > 0 that also fall inside the PROB_LGBM_V2 ≥ 0.362 mask.



Map of Training Points.




2.1.3 Peat Inventory Data
The Minnesota Peat Inventory contains lab data that was used for the carbon and organic decomposition models. First, all tables were merged into a horizon-level master table on site ID so that ash, carbon, bulk density, and classification were on the same table. The table had 35,142 horizons from 7,032 unique pedons. Missing top or bottom depths in horizons were filled using adjacent horizons when possible. Horizons that could not be corrected were flagged and then either extended to the next horizon or a max depth of 200cm. SOC and Db were then gap filled using the best method available based on existing data:

2.1.3.1 Gap Filling

Measured lab data: used when available (SOC: 533 horizons, BD: 3,209 horizons).
Ash regression: with horizons that were missing SOC or BD but had ash content, a linear regression (SOC-Ash and BD-Ash) was fit and used to predict the missing value (SOC-Ash R²=0.623; BD-Ash R²=0.579).
Random Forest: a random forest model was trained on von Post decomposition class, top/mid horizon depth, and horizon classification (Fibric, Hemic, Sapric). This performed poorly (SOC CV R²=‑0.051).
Still missing: horizons with no von Post score either were left unfilled and excluded from carbon stock calculation

Because the rf fill performed poorly this was determined to be a property of the data as the SOC in peat stays relatively constant (mean 50.67% and a std of 4.77%). So there is little variance for the rf features to explain. Db was found to be more variable than SOC and a class mean fill for Db would have more uncertainty than SOC. After gap filling was complete the filled values were flagged by the method used to track data quality: Tier 1: no RF-filled values used (measured or ash-regression only, 503 pedons, 13.1%) Tier 2: some RF-filled values (under 50% of horizons, 202 pedons, 5.3%) Tier 3: majority RF-filled (over 50% of horizons, 3,123 pedons, 81.6%)

title: 3  Covariate Curation
text:
3.0.1 Computing Environment
Processing of covariates was done on the Minnesota Supercomputing Institute (MSI) Agate AMD EPYC Linux cluster. A majority of scripts were run using SLURM batch scheduling. A custom conda environment (gdalenvgeospat) was created on MSI to run packages including GDAL, rasterio, fiona, geopandas, and WhiteboxTools. Standard MSI environments were not used to process rasters because of conflicts between system GDAL and the conda installed GDAL.


3.0.2 Reference Grid
All rasters were aligned to the gNATSGO grid before modeling. This process was done using gdalwarp with -ts 66474 75185 (target size) and -te (target extent) flags. Bilinear resampling was used for continuous data and nearest neighbor was used for categorical data.
Reference raster: gNATSGO 10m MUKEY raster Dimensions: 66,474 × 75,185 pixels CRS: EPSG:5070 (NAD83 / Conus Albers Equal Area) Origin: −99,098, 3,021,389 Resolution: 10m


3.0.3 Digital Elevation Model
Source: USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), 10m resolution Download: National Map Downloader, https://apps.nationalmap.gov/downloader/ Tiles mosaicked into a single statewide raster and clipped to the Minnesota state boundary using GDAL warp with output CRS forced to EPSG:5070 minnesota_dem_10m.tif


3.0.4 Terrain Derivatives (WhiteboxTools)
WhiteboxTools v2.4.0 was accessed through Python API with a conda kernel configured on MSI. Standard Python/GDAL environments on MSI did not include WhiteboxTools so the gdalenvgeospat environment was used. Multiprocessing parallelization (multiprocessing.Pool) was used to run terrain derivatives at the same time to speed up the process.


3.0.5 Processing Strategy
Two approaches were used depending if the derivative is affected by watershed context: Statewide: Computed directly on the statewide mosaicked DEM. These derivatives only require local information and do not depend on upstream drainage areas. slope, aspect, hillshade planCurvature, profileCurvature, meanCurvature, maximalCurvature geomorphons, pennockLandformClass devfrommeanelev (4m, 8m, 16m), diffFromMeanElev relativeTopographicPosition (4m, 8m, 16m) By HUC8 watershed: For derivatives that are impacted by water flow, a different approach was used. Minnesota was divided into 127 HUC8 watersheds and a 5km buffer was applied to each HUC8 polygon to prevent edge effects. Derivatives were computed on each buffered watershed tile independently with individual SLURM jobs and then mosaicked back together with the overlapping buffer areas removed. breached_dem (hydrologically conditioned DEM) d8FlowAccumulation, dInfFlowAccumulation wetnessIndex (TWI)


3.0.6 Hydrological Modification
Peatlands often exist in low-lying poorly drained areas. When preparing a DEM for hydrological analysis, artificial depressions in the DEM are removed so that waterflow can run continuously throughout the landscape. A breaching method was used to carve channels through barriers blocking drainage. This allows water to flow continuously through the model, producing more accurate flow accumulation and wetness index values. Modification workflow by HUC8 watershed: Step Tool Output Purpose 1 FillSingleCellPits _01_fscp.tif Remove single-cell LiDAR artifacts 2 FlattenLakes _02_flat.tif Flatten lake surfaces to minimum elevation 3 TopologicalBreachBurn _03_tbb.tif Burn stream network into DEM 4 BreachDepressionsLeastCost _04_bdlc.tif Breach through road embankments and barriers 5 FillSingleCellPits _05_fel.tif Final cleanup
Parameters: TopologicalBreachBurn snap = 2.0m (2-cell tolerance at 1m resolution for stream/DEM alignment) BreachDepressionsLeastCost dist = 100 cells (100m max breach length), max_cost = 1.0m Input datasets: Lakes: DNR HydroFeatures (polygons) Streams: DNR RiversStreams (lines) Roads: MnDOT Roadway Routes (lines) Final terrain derivatives: slope.tif, aspect.tif, hillshade.tif, planCurvature.tif, profileCurvature.tif, maximalCurvature.tif, breached_dem.tif, d8FlowAccumulation.tif, dInfFlowAccumulation.tif, wetnessIndex.tif, devfrommeanelev_4m.tif, devfrommeanelev_8m.tif, devfrommeanelev_16m.tif, diffFromMeanElev.tif, relativeTopographicPosition_4m.tif, relativeTopographicPosition_8m.tif, relativeTopographicPosition_16m.tif, geomorphons.tif, pennockLandformClass.tif


3.0.7 Sentinel-2 Imagery
Source: COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED from Google Earth Engine Dates: 2019–2024 Extent: Minnesota state boundary (TIGER/2018/States) Seasonal Compositing Three seasonal median composites were generated: Spring (April–May): cloud and snow masked Summer (June–August): cloud masked Fall (September–October): cloud and snow masked Cloud masking used SCL layer excluding: cloud shadows (class 3), medium cloud (class 8), high cloud (class 9), thin cirrus (class 10). Per-image pre-filter excluded scenes >30% cloud cover. Snow/ice (class 11) masked for spring and fall.
In total there were 10 bands per season: B02, B03, B04, B05, B06, B07, B08, B8A, B11, B12 and 2 additional bands were calculated: NDVI = (B08 − B04) / (B08 + B04) Normalized Difference Vegetation Index to quantify vegetation health and density SWDI = from Green (B03) and Red Edge 1 (B05) Soil Water Deficit Index sensitive to surface moisture Bands that were originally at a 20m resolution (B05–B08A, B11, B12) were resampled to 10m during the GEE export.


3.0.8 Sentinel 2 Export and Mosaicking
GEE automatically tiled the whole state exports. Tiles were downloaded from google drive to a local machine then uploaded into the MSI project. Once in MSI, tiles were mosaicked into a single multiband tiff file using gdal_merge.py. LZW compression, internal tiling, and BIGTIFF were used to merge the outputs.


3.0.9 Tasseled Cap
Tasseled Cap Transformation compresses multiband data into single bands that can better track soils, urban areas, and vegetation (source). The three components used in this project were the Brightness (TCB), Greenness (TCG), and wetness (TCW). These bands are computed by applying a coefficient to existing S2 bands (Nedkov, 2017). Tasseled cap bands were computed on MSI and validated on expected correlation patterns (positive Brightness–Greenness, negative Brightness–Wetness, stronger Greenness–Wetness correlation in summer vs. spring/fall)


3.0.10 Sentinel-1
The final probability and depth models use the combined (ascending and descending) Sentinel-1 composites (s1_spring_combined, s1_summer_combined and s1_fall_combined). The original export from GEE separated ascending and descending passes and had incomplete coverage in ascending data. Only 43% of points in the model had S1 coverage. However, the S1 covariate survived recursive feature elimination (RFE) in initial Random Forest model runs and increased R2 values. The export was changed to combine ascending and descending runs and to extend the date range, which gave the combined covariates used in the final models.
Three bands per composite: VV (dB), VH (dB), VV/VH ratio. Exported as INT16 scaled ×100, converted to float32 /100 during mosaicking.


3.0.11 PRISM Climate Data
Source: PRISM Climate Group, 30-year normals at 800m Layers: Annual precipitation, mean July max temp, mean annual temp, mean January min temp
PRISM data was reprojected to EPSG:5070, clipped to the DEM extent, and resampled to 10m (bilinear) during alignment to the reference grid.


3.0.12 National Wetlands Inventory (NWI)
Source: NWI geodatabase (https://www.mngeo.state.mn.us/chouse/water_wetlands.html)
The NWI vector data was converted and classified to a raster on MSI using fiona and rasterio. Polygons were classified by their Cowardin code and separated into 3 distinct groupings: 0 = Non-wetland 1 = Wetland 2 = Lowland conifer (PFO4, PSS4, PFO2, PSS2, mixed codes containing “/4”)
The encoding classes were evaluated during initial random forest model runs and the 3-class classification gave no improvement. The final raster used was split into a binary encoding where 0 = non-wetland, 1 = any wetland


3.0.13 Distance Features
Source: Minnesota statewide vector datasets Roads: MnDOT Roadway Routes Streams/rivers: DNR RiversStreams Water bodies: DNR HydroFeatures
Euclidean distance rasters were computed from vector layers using GDAL proximity.


3.0.14 gNATSGO Organic Soils
Source: gNATSGO for Minnesota
gNATSGO (gridded National Soil Survey Geographic Database) is the USDAs Natural Resource Conservation Service’s soils product. It merges SSURGO with STATSGO into one database per state. The 10m MUKEY raster was used to pull organic soils classified in Minnesota and then split into 8 separate classes based on soil taxonomy: 0: Non-organic 1: Shallow Peat (histic epipedon, non-Histosol, 20–40cm organic) 2: Terric Saprists 3: Terric Hemists 4: Terric Fibrists 5: Typic Saprists 6: Typic Hemists 7: Typic Fibrists 8: Sphagno Histosols
A binary version of this raster was also created using any MUKEY containing an organic component.
Both gNATSGO derived layers ended up being excluded from probability model training as predictors because they are peat classification products and including them caused circular logic. They were retained as reference/validation layers and used in peat property models.


3.0.15 Categorical Layers
These layers produced visible polygon shaped artifacts such as geometric edges in the spatial inferences. Because the models learned to change predictions on polygon edges they were excluded from training.
10m_quaternary_geology.tif — Quaternary Geology classification pennockLandformClass.tif — Pennock Landform Class geomorphons.tif — geomorphon landform classification
The AUC cost from removal of these covariates was found to be minimal in experimentation (~0.002) and the visual output quality improved.

title: 4  4. Model Implementation
text:
4.1 4.1 Overview
This section covers the development and evaluation of models created to predict peat presence and other characteristics. The modeling workflow has four steps: (1) curation of the training data for each property that is being modeled. (2) covariate feature selection. (3) model training and hyperparameter tuning. (4) model evaluation.
In total, four statewide raster maps were produced including the probability of peat presence, peat depth, the composition of the upper meter of peat as fibric, hemic, and sapric percent, and carbon stock. The final probability, depth, and composition models use a LightGBM algorithm. The carbon stock map was then calculated from the depth map using a linear depth–carbon stock curve. Earlier model versions and other algorithms that were tested are documented alongside the selected production models.

title: 4  4. Model Implementation
text:
4.1.1 Cross-Validation
Cross-validation is a method used in machine learning to evaluate the performance of a model. Two cross-validation strategies were used in development and are reported with each model’s results.

4.1.1.1 Random cross-validation
Random cross-validation used stratified k-fold splitting (k=5) and randomly assigned observations to folds. This approach is a standard method in machine learning but it can create bias when training points that are clustered. Because nearby points often have similar covariate values, a randomly held out point may be geographically close to a training point which allows the model to interpolate on nearby data. This can inflate the metrics used to evaluate the effectiveness of models.


4.1.1.2 Spatial block cross-validation
Spatial block cross-validation was used to replicate independent validation. The boundary of the project area (Minnesota) was split into a 50 km x 50 km grid. All training points that shared a block were assigned to the same fold and then blocks were allocated to folds in a round robin fashion. When a block is held out for validation, the model has never seen any training point within that geographic area forcing generalization across space. This method produces a lower but more reliable estimate. The performance drop from the random to spatial cross-validation in the results shows spatial autocorrelation that is occurring in the training data.



4.1.2 Shared Modeling Decisions
Some decisions made in the modeling workflow were consistent across all target properties and model types:

CRS - All training points and covariates are projected to Albers Equal Area Conic NAD83 (EPSG:5070)
Missing Data - Covariate features with missing data at training point locations were imputed with the column median from training data only. This affected distance features at edge locations and Sentinel-1 features where coverage was incomplete.
Negative prediction clipping - The depth regression models tested (XGBoost, LightGBM, GAM, SVM) can sometimes produce negative predictions which is unrealistic because peat depth can not be negative. All negative predictions were clipped to zero.
Output encoding - Raster map inferences were written as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) at a 10m resolution. Percentage outputs rasters are stored as uint8 (value × 0.5 = percent) and the depth raster as uint16 (1cm per unit)

title: 4  4. Model Implementation
text:
4.2 4.2 Peat Probability
The peat probability modeling workflow has two distinct versions. The first version (V1) was a random forest. The second (V2) used a gradient boosting algorithm (LightGBM) and produced the final model used to create the map displayed in the MNLCC viewer. The random forest work is kept within this documentation because it informs training data decisions and because the comparison algorithms were tested alongside it.

4.2.1 Training Data
The peat probability models were trained on the peat binary presence/absence dataset compiled from the MN DNR Peat Inventory, NASIS, and the MBS. The initial compiled dataset contained ~102,000 points. After shallow, non-histosol points with organic material depths of 1-20 cm were excluded, the final training dataset contained 57,134 points with 18.2% coded as peat and 81.8% as non peat.


4.2.2 Covariate Development and Categorical Features
The initial V1 covariate stack was made up of 172 candidate features. To limit the redundancy of predictors in the random forest model, a Pearson correlation filter was applied using a threshold of |r| ≥ 0.90. Each pair of correlated features meeting that threshold had the lower variance feature dropped from the stack. This filtering reduced the set to 143 covariates.

4.2.2.1 Exclusion of Peat Reference Layers
Early model runs (exp201, exp301-303) included peat reference layers as predictive features such as the Potentially Wet Histosol layer and gNATSGO organic components. These experiments resulted in inflated AUC values (exp201 AUC=0.994) because the model was learning to reproduce the reference maps instead of independently predicting peat presence from the covariates. To prevent the model from using circular logic the peat reference maps were ultimately excluded from the feature set.


4.2.2.2 Categorical covariates and polygon artifacts
Other early experiments (exp401-408) included categorical raster layers encoded as one-hot features: quaternary geology classification, Pennock landform class, and geomorphons. The inclusion of these covariates in the model resulted in visible polygon shaped artifacts in the output inferences such as hard geometric edges that corresponded to vector boundaries. Because the boundaries were showing mapped units rather than a continuous peat forming process, the model learned to abruptly change predictions at polygon edges.
In exp409 and exp410, all categorical one-hot features were removed. This cost minimal AUC (0.974 with categoricals, 0.9722 without) and substantially improved the visual quality of the inference map. Exp410 was selected as the production RF peat probability model because of its metric scores as well as visual coherence.


4.2.2.3 National Wetlands Inventory Encoding
Three NWI encoding strategies were evaluated across RF model experiments - 3-class encoding (0=non-wetland, 1=wetland, 2=lowland conifer) 403, 406 - Binary encoding (0=non-wetland, 1=any wetland class) 404, 407 - NWI excluded entirely 405, 408
NWI contributed minimally to the overall model AUC on experiments using the original full point dataset. On the revised 1-20 cm dropped point dataset the AUC differences were negligible between NWI encoding strategies (AUC 0.973 versus 0.974). NWI Binary encoding was selected to be kept in the final RF model because it preserved visually meaningful wetland versus non-wetland discrimination without creating artifacts.



4.2.3 Random Forest (V1)

4.2.3.1 Recursive Feature elimination
After the Pearson coefficient was applied and categorical features were dropped (excluding NWI binary) recursive feature elimination (RFE) was applied to reduce the remaining covariates used in the model. A random forest classifier with 200 trees was trained using 5-fold cross validation. Iterations of the model were run and the feature with the lowest mean impurity-based importance across folds was dropped each time. This process was continued until AUC was reduced by more than 0.5 points from the maximum, resulting in a final stack of 41 features to be used in the RF model.
The set of the 41 final features includes:

All 12 sentinel-2 spring bands
Selected summer and fall bands
Tasseled Cap components for all seasons
Terrain derivatives (DEM, slope, wetness index, flow accumulation, curvature, deviation from mean elevation)
PRISM climate normals
NWI binary wetland indicator
Distance features (to water, streams, roads, waterbody edge)

Exp410 was chosen as the final random forest production model. It used the 41 features with 500 trees and a minimum of 1 sample per leaf.

The decrease from random cv (AUC=0.972) to spatial cv (AUC=0.957) shows spatial autocorrelation in the training data where nearby observations are more similar and random folds are overestimating performance.



4.2.4 Gradient Boosting (V2)
Version 2 of the peat probability modeling process used gradient boosting algorithms. Gradient boosting builds a model as a sequence of decision trees where each new tree is trained to correct the errors by the trees before it. Gradient boosting can fit complicated patterns between covariates more closely than a random forest, but is prone to overfitting if settings and tuning are not controlled.
Two boosting implementations were tested in this project, XGBoost and LightGBM. Both were trained on the covariates that remained after the Pearson correlation filter (|r| ≥ 0.90) was applied. Recursive feature elimination was not used for the boosting models. It is only needed for the random forest because the boosted models select correlated covariates as trees are built.
The peat present points are the minority class in the training data (18.2% of the 57,134 points). Because of this, weighted and unweighted versions of both boosting algorithms were compared. In the weighted version of the model runs, the peat class has more influence in the training. The ‘scale_pos_weight’ setting was set at 4.495 which is the ratio of non-peat to peat points so that they have an equal total weight. This helps the model identify the less common class, in this case peat presence, but can overestimate the likelihood of that class. In the unweighted versions each point counts equally and the model learns the natural frequency. The imbalance is then handled afterward when a probability threshold is selected. Weighting had little effect on the overall model performance. Spatial AUC scores were almost the same between weighted and unweighted models for both XGBoost (0.9730 vs. 0.9738) and LightGBM (0.9744 vs. 0.9739). However, the unweighted models had better Brier scores and higher F1 scores for both algorithms. Because the final maps show predicted probabilities and the classification threshold is applied afterward, unweighted models were used for all final probability maps.


4.2.5 Generalized Additive Model (GAM)
A generalized additive model (GAM) fits a curve for each covariate and then adds those curves together. For the target of peat presence, a logistic GAM was used. A GAM can identify patterns occurring in a single covariate such as peat presence becoming more likely below a certain slope. However, unlike a random forest or boosted models, a standard GAM does not identify interactions between covariates.
A logistic GAM was built using the pygam library with thin-plate spline terms, which allow the model to fit smooth curves to individual covariates. A GAM with this many smooth terms requires a lot of memory, so each cross-validation fold was trained on a balanced subsample of 30,000 observations (15,000 peat, 15,000 non-peat).

4.2.6 Support Vector Machine
A support vector machine (SVM) identifies the boundary that separates peat and non-peat observations that have the widest margin. A radial basis function (RBF) kernel was used which allows the boundary to be a curve rather than a straight line. Because SVM uses distances between observations, StandardScaler was used to standardize covariates so that no variable would have an advantage on the model. A large amount of memory is required to run these models which increases with the number of training points, so each fold used a subsample that included 15,000 observations (7,500 peat, 7,500 non-peat). Predictions were then generated on the full held-out fold. Hyperparameters were C = 1.0, gamma = ‘scale’ and class_weight = ‘balanced’.

4.2.7 Logistic Regression
Logistic regression predicts the likelihood of peat presence based on a weighted combination of the covariates. It assumes each covariate has a straight-line relationship with peat presence and does not account for thresholds. In this case, logistic regression was used primarily as a baseline to compare to the more complex models. The model is standardized with StandardScaler, uses the lbfgs solver, C = 1.0 and class_weight = ‘balanced’.

4.2.8 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a type of neural network commonly used with images and other spatial data. It learns patterns such as edges and textures and then combines those patterns to make a prediction. In this project the raster covariates acted as a “landscape” surrounding the points to then be used to predict from rather than using individual pixel values. The model used two inputs; 1) a raster patch on each training point and 2) the covariate values inside of the patch. These inputs were processed separately and then combined to make a prediction. Two patch sizes were tested (15 × 15 and 31 × 31) which changed the amount of pixels the model saw surrounding the points. The best CNN model had a spatial CV AUC of 0.962 which was similar to the boosted models. The CNN was not chosen as the production model because it required large compute and compute time. Mapping was also more complex because the spatial inference requires a full raster patch around every pixel.


4.2.9 Final Model: LightGBM
After all of the above models were tested, LightGBM was selected as the best performing based on its spatial AUC score and Brier score.

4.2.9.1 Model settings
The final hyperparameters came from Optuna tuning of the LightGBM model. In the tuning process the largest gains in performance came from slower learning rates and stronger larger minimum leaf sizes. The final settings of the LightGBM peat probability model are:

620 trees (n_estimators) with a learning rate of 0.0166 so each tree makes only a small correction
up to 282 leaves per tree with a maximum depth of 15, and at least 92 points in each leaf (min_child_samples)
each tree uses 56% of the rows (subsample) and 72% of the features (colsample_bytree)
L1 regularization (reg_alpha) of 3.38 and L2 regularization (reg_lambda) of 0.71, which penalizes large leaf values
trained unweighted, on all 57,134 points



4.2.9.2 Covariates
The final model uses 57 covariates:

terrain: slope, aspect, hillshade, three curvatures, breached DEM, D-infinity flow accumulation, deviation from mean elevation and relative topographic position (at three scales each)
distance to water and streams (roads was removed due to artifacts)
PRISM climate normals
Sentinel-2 bands and Tasseled Cap brightness, greenness and wetness
Sentinel-1 combined VV, VH and VV/VH ratio composites
the NWI wetland classes



4.2.9.3 Performance
Spatial cross-validation gives the performance that can be expected in areas without training points:

At the selected threshold (0.362), the spatial out-of-fold predictions found 8,551 of the 10,397 peat points (recall 0.822) and labeled 2,003 of the 46,737 non-peat points as peat (4.3%). Of all points that were predicted as peat, 81% were peat (precision 0.810), giving an F1 score of 0.816 and an overall accuracy of 93.3%.


4.2.9.4 Variable importance
Two measures of importance were calculated for the probability model, split counts and gain. The split counts show how often the model uses a covariate and gain shows how much the covariate improves the model’s fit. By split count the most used covariates were two PRISM climate layers (precipitation and January minimum temperature) along with the breached DEM and the distances to water and streams. Using gain, slope is the most important covariate by a large margin (over four times the second) followed by NWI non-wetland class and PRISM January minimum temperature.
add in table of covariate importance



4.2.10 Threshold Selection
The final probability model produces a value between 0 and 1 for every pixel in the map raster. To convert this product into a binary peat or non-peat mask, a threshold needs to be selected. The threshold is the cutoff value of which pixel values that are higher are assigned a value of peat present and values below that threshold turn into peat absent. Moving the threshold changes the total area of peatlands mapped. For example, moving the threshold from 0.25 to 0.50 changes the mapped peatland area from around 9.2 million to 6.3 million acres.

4.2.10.1 Final threshold
Using a single metric to derive a threshold can favor one kind of error so the final threshold uses five metrics. The out-of-fold predictions were swept across 500 cutoffs (0.01–0.99) and the optimal threshold of each metric was found:



Metric
Optimal threshold




Youden’s J
0.161


Balanced accuracy
0.161


F1
0.362


Accuracy
0.466


Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)

The range in optimal threshold from the above metrics range because they weigh mistakes differently. Youden’s J and balanced accuracy count the peat and non-peat classes equally so they favor a low threshold that catches a majority of peat but with a higher amount of false positives. Accuracy and MCC are more influenced by the more prevalent non-peat classes and favor a higher threshold. F1 is in the middle because it looks at how well the peat class itself is predicted. Taking the median of the five, 0.362, avoids committing to either extreme.
The 0.362 threshold is then used to produce the statewide peat mask. The mapped peatland extent within Minnesota is 7,553,829 acres (3,056,926 ha; 30,569 km²).

title: 4  4. Model Implementation
text:
4.3 4.3 Peat Depth
The peat depth model predicts the thickness of peat in centimeters at every pixel inside the peat mask from the probability model. The target (depb), is the maximum peat depth measured at a point. Because depth is a regression problem the model predicts a continuous number and not a class. Depth is an important property in this project because below ground carbon depends on how much peat is present, and the final below ground carbon stock map is calculated directly from the depth map.
Peat depth is a harder variable to predict than peat presence. The covariate stack used are surface properties that can describe peat presence well but the thickness of peat underground is only indirectly related to them. Depth is also strongly clustered in space which can be seen in the gap between random and spatial cross-validation. Two measures are reported for the depth models:
R² - the share of the variation in depth that the model explains Mean Absolute Error (MAE) - The average miss in centimeters.

4.3.1 Training Data and Masking
Early depth models were trained on the full point set which included points that had a depth of zero. This produced deceptively high R² values (~0.70), a misleading result because the high R² mainly showed the model separating zero from non-zero depth, and the model had bad accuracy at locations that actually have peat.
To correct this problem a two-stage approach was used. First, the peat probability model is used as a mask, and depth regression is trained and predicted only on locations the probability model classifies as peat. For a depth point to be included in the training data it must meet both of the criterion depb > 0 AND PROB_LGBM ≥ 0.362. This filter resulted in 8,223 training points.


4.3.2 Early Random Forest Experiments
The depth modeling originally used a random forest model. Experiments that were tested included adding SSURGO soil survey data as a covariate, dropping shallow peat (1-20 cm) points from the training data, and log-transforming the depth target. Recursive feature elimination reduced the feature set to 15 with performance improving as features were removed. The random CV R² started at 0.4233 with 125 features and increased to 0.484 with 15 features.


4.3.3 Other Algorithms
XGBoost, LightGBM, GAM, a linear SVM and Ridge regression were also evaluated for depth in the same way as probability. On spatial CV the models performed similarly with an R² between 0.26 and 0.33. The random CV R² of the gradient boosting models was much higher than their spatial CV R² (0.62 versus 0.30) showing that peat depth is even more spatially correlated than peat probability.


4.3.4 Final Base Model: LightGBM
The depth pipeline followed the same steps as probability. First a correlation filter reduced 172 features down to 143. RFE was run for the random forest only (143 reduced to 37). Baseline training of the models and then tuning with Optuna (TPE sampler, 50 trials per model, optimizing spatial CV R²). No class weighting was needed for a regression target.
LightGBM was the best performing model before and after tuning. The untuned spatial R² values were 0.27 (random forest), 0.28 (XGBoost) and 0.29 (LightGBM), and after tuning they were 0.2731, 0.2885 and 0.2925. The final base model, DEPTH_LGBM_TUNED, has a spatial R² of 0.2925 and MAE of 74.6 cm, a random R² of 0.4273 and MAE of 66.1 cm, and was trained on 8,223 points.
The depth model uses the same covariate exclusion list as probability with one difference. The SSURGO organic soil classes are kept for depth. They are a peat classification product, so they would be circular for predicting whether peat exists, but because depth is only trained inside the peat present mask using this layer for peat depth it is not circular, and it improved the depth models.


4.3.5 Deep-Tail Blend

4.3.5.1 Predicting Deep Peat
The base LGBM model underpredicted deep peat. Training point data has depths up to 900 cm with 677 points deeper than 366 cm and 179 points deeper than 490 cm, which made up about 10% of the training set. Because a LightGBM model predicts the mean of the training points in each leaf, the rare deep observations get averaged together with shallower neighbors, which causes the model to underestimate areas where deep peat exists.
